I pulled the initial trace Ivan sent and ran it against our flow correlator. Summary of what I'm seeing:

- Flows that fail show a period of consistent data transfer followed by an abrupt RST originating from the customer edge IP (not our endpoints). Packet sequence numbers indicate the RST is unsolicited from the path.
- A subset of failing sessions share identical source ports on the customer side across different worker connections. That pattern + your note about a recent capacity increase points to SNAT port reuse at the edge.
- There are intermittent ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages visible, usually when the payload spikes above ~1200B after TLS record aggregation. I suspect an MTU/fragmentation interaction, but the RST origin suggests active stateful device involvement.

Hypothesis: Your edge firewall is doing source NAT to a small ephemeral port pool and aggressively reusing ports, causing collisions. Combined with MTU-triggered retransmits and state aging (short TCP idle timers) that can surface as mid-stream RSTs when the re-used port maps to a new flow.

Immediate mitigations to test:
- Temporarily increase ephemeral port range on your edge (recommended: 32768-60999)
- Raise NAT session limit / increase TCP idle timeout to >=120s for flows to Redwood
- Enable source port preservation (if your vendor supports it) when load-balancing outbound connections
- If possible, add a static 1:1 SNAT for a small pool of workers to test (reduces collisions)

I attached a quick snapshot (edge-snat-snapshot.txt) showing the port collision pattern and our annotated correlation. If you can run a pcap that includes the pre-RST sequence and the device's translated IP/port, that will confirm.

Marissa — thanks for the analysis. We pulled the firewall logs and confirmed: the PaloEdge cluster was configured with a default ephemeral pool that collapsed during concurrent bursts; NAT session timeout was set to 30s for outbound sessions. We increased the ephemeral range, bumped timeout to 180s, and enabled source port preservation on the outbound load-balancer.

Attached is a pcap (acme_pcap_capture.pcap) that captures the same failing flow pre-change and a follow-up capture post-change showing no RST after 60s during the same workload.

We'll keep this change for 72 hours and report back, but early signs are good. Thanks for the quick guidance.

— Acme Ops Team
